paragraphs.source_en: The successive Mesolithic period was much drier and the lakes in the lowlands had probably dried up by the end of the 9th millennium BP (Cremaschi 1998). The drying event that began at around 8,500 BP forced humans to abandon the lowlands and concentrate in the mountains where water supplies were still available (Di Lernia 1997). Pollen evidence suggests that a significant cultural change took place during this period when people began to experiment with new subsistence strategies based on wild cereals (Castelletti et al. 1998). The intensive exploitation of mainly vegetal resources is attested by the predominance of a macrolithic industry and by a considerable increase in stone grinding technology. It is difficult to imagine a substantial presence of large water-dependent animals in the drier lowlands, although they may have still been present on a seasonal basis.

paragraphs.source_en: Which of these two Early Holocene phases would have been the most probable starting point for the Round Head paintings? Scholars supporting the high chronology generally consider the beginning of this artistic tradition to have been in the Mesolithic period (Sansoni 1994; Di Lernia 1997). They are basing this on indirect evidence from excavations, such as a wooden spatula with traces of red ochre on the smoothed extremity, which was found at Uan Afuda and dated to 8,790 BP. In the same shelter ten grinding stones bearing traces of red ochre were also unearthed from the Mesolithic layers (Castelletti, et al. 1998). Since these coloured objects were discovered in a shelter decorated with Round Head paintings, a relationship between them has been proposed (Mori 2000).
